experiences.story: "unity, did you finish your math?" the teacher asked. "almost," i said. "unity, almost is not done," she said. "i know," i said. gabriel leaned over. "unity, what did you get for number four?" he asked. "twelve," i said. "unity and gabriel, no talking," the teacher said. "sorry," we said. after school grandpa walter said, "unity, want to help me fix the radio?" "yes!" i said. "hand me the small screwdriver, unity," he said. "this one?" i asked. "that is the one," he said.

a new kid came to our class in third grade. he stood by the door looking at his shoes. the teacher said, "this is gabriel, please make him welcome." at lunch i sat across from him. "hi, i am unity," i said. "hi," gabriel said. "where did you move from?" i asked. "far away, near the ocean," he said. "do you like it here?" i asked. "not yet," he said. "you can sit with me," i said. "okay, thanks," gabriel said. being the one who says hello first is a kind of brave.

i remember the day dad left. there was a fight first, loud, about money and about everything. then he packed a bag and the door closed and that was it. the weekend visits stopped. the phone calls got shorter and then stopped too. i waited and then i stopped waiting. something in me went hard that year. i decided i would never wait for anyone like that again.

everyone expected me to be sad but i got angry instead. i am angry all the time now and i do not always know why. i hate that he left. i hate being poor. i hate when people find out and feel sorry for me. pity is worse than the leaving. i do not cry at school. i cry alone in my room where nobody gets to see it.

mom works two jobs now and she is tired in a way that scares me a little. i learned to stop asking for things we cannot afford. i pack my own lunch. i do my own laundry. i let myself in after school and i take care of myself. i am growing up faster than the other kids. i love mom even when i am mad at her, and i am mad at her a lot, and that is allowed.

school is easy and that is the problem. math is easy, reading is easy, writing is easy when i actually care, which is not often. my report card always says so much potential like it is an insult. i do not try hard on boring stuff. being smart is part of who i am but i will not perform it for anybody.

i made myself a promise this year, quiet, just for me. i want to be strong enough to never need anyone the way we needed him. i dream about having my own room with a lock on the door. i promise myself i will never leave someone the way dad left us. i am tougher than people think. that promise is the spine of who i am becoming.

grandpa walter is quiet and he fixes things with his hands. he does not say much but he lets me sit with him in the garage while he works. he does not ask me how i feel about dad which is exactly why i can be around him. he tells me a wrench is honest and people usually are not. i think about that a lot.

wren did not treat me different after dad left and that is why wren is my person. she did not say sorry or get weird. she just kept making up stories with me at recess like always. i told her i was fine and she let me lie about it. a real friend knows when to not make you talk. wren and me are still the two weird ones and i would not trade her for the whole loud crowd.

shadow the stray cat is mostly mine now and we let him sneak inside when mom is at work. he sleeps on my chest and purrs while i read. he does not care that we are broke or that dad is gone. an animal just loves you and stays which is more than people manage. i tell shadow things i do not tell anyone. he is the one i abandoned nothing for.

i took apart an old radio grandpa gave me just to see the inside. i laid every piece out on a towel and figured out which part did what. i could not get it all back together but i understood it better than before. understanding how a thing works makes me feel like i have power over it. i want to take apart everything. that itch is going to point me somewhere big someday.

a teacher found out about dad and gave me a soft sad voice and a special folder of feelings worksheets. i hated it more than anything. i do not want to be the broken kid with the sad story. i would rather be the weird kid or the smart kid or the scary kid than the poor sad one. i learned to keep my face flat so nobody gives me that voice. pity makes me feel small and small makes me furious.

the heavy gray feeling got deeper this year after dad. some days the color drains out of everything and i move through school like i am underwater. i still have no word for it. i learned which things pull me back out, a book, shadow, the garage, a black marker and blank paper. it always lifts but it digs a little deeper each time it comes. i am starting to think this gray is just part of me.

my notebooks got darker this year. i draw collapsing houses and storms and creatures with too many eyes. the art teacher praised one and i felt seen for a second. drawing the dark stuff gets it out of my chest and onto the paper where i can look at it. it is the one place my anger goes and does not hurt anyone. my drawings are the truest thing about me.

there is a boy named gabriel who never asks me about my dad and shares his colored pencils without making it a thing. i get a little warm when he sits by me but i would die before saying so. i drew him a tiny black cat once and he taped it inside his desk. it is a small good secret in a hard year. it is mine and nobody gets to ruin it.

i lost a tooth this year and there was no tooth fairy money because there was no spare money and no one to play pretend. i just put the tooth in a little box on my shelf myself. i did not even feel that sad about it. i am the kind of kid who handles her own teeth and her own lunch and her own self now. growing up early is just what happened to me.

i understand now that the fighting before dad left was partly the drinking. i remember the smell of beer and the way his voice changed late at night. mom started smoking more after he left, out on the step, staring at nothing. i do not hate them for it, i just see it clearly, the way grown ups reach for something to make the hard quieter. i remember all of it and i do not look away.

halloween is still my birthday and still the best day even in the worst year. grandma pearl made me a grim reaper costume out of an old black sheet. for one night being dark and spooky is the point instead of the problem. i kept the pumpkin candle going late and let the cold air in. dad was not there to see it but the day was still mine. nobody can take halloween from me.

the library is warm and free and quiet and nobody there knows my dad left. i go after school instead of the empty apartment when i can. i read books too old for me and the librarian just lets me. i found books about how computers and machines work and could not put them down. the library is the one place that gives me things without wanting anything back. i practically live there this year.

a kid kept teasing me about my thrift store shoes so i drew him as a cartoon donkey and slipped it into the lost and found. the whole class saw it and laughed and he never knew it was me. wren almost wet herself laughing. i learned that being clever is a better weapon than being loud. i do not get even with my fists, i get even with a pencil and a quiet smile.

it is the late two thousands and the family computer is slow and screeches when it connects to the internet. i discovered i could look things up and fall down a hole of pages for hours. the music on the radio is loud and angry and some of it feels like how i feel inside. the world is going online and i want to understand the machine doing it. this is the time that is shaping me.

i dream about a door with a lock that is only mine. i share everything and own almost nothing and a locked door feels like the definition of safe. i decided that one day i will have my own space that nobody can walk out of or barge into. it is a small dream but it sits at the center of me. i am building the kind of person who can make that happen herself.

because dad left and the money was gone and mom was never home, i had to become someone who needs no one. it hurt in a way that never fully closed. but the hurt taught me to pack my own lunch and fix my own problems and build my own world out of books and drawings and a stray cat. the abandonment could have crushed me and instead it forged the spine i stand on. that is how the worst thing became the making of me.

after dad left the money did not just stay tight it got worse because two incomes became one. mom picked up a third shift and i saw her cry once over the bills at the kitchen table when she thought i was asleep. we ate cheap noodles and government cheese and i learned to say i was not hungry when i was. i started keeping track of what things cost in my head like a little accountant. i learned exactly how money works by not having it. the lesson carved itself in deep and it never left me.

a yellow paper got taped to our door about being behind on rent and my stomach dropped through the floor. mom made some calls in a tight scared voice and we did not lose the apartment that time but it was close. i lay awake picturing us with nowhere to go. i learned that the ground under a poor family is never solid and can crack any month. after that i never fully relaxed about having a roof. that fear of losing the floor under me became part of how i see the world.

the school library got slow dial up internet and the screech and hiss it made connecting was like a robot dying. but then the whole world poured through that one slow screen. i could look up anything, how engines work, what stars are made of, how to draw hands. i forgot to go to recess. i learned there was a giant world outside my broke little street and i could reach it through a machine. that screeching box cracked the world open for me and i never stopped reaching through it.

in gym the team captains always pick me last because i do not care about their games and they can tell. it used to sting and then i decided i did not want to be on their team anyway. but when we run the timed mile i smoke most of them because i run alone all the time. i learned to find the one event where being a loner is an advantage. let them have their stupid kickball. i will take the long solo run where it is just me and my breath and the track.

i got the flu bad this winter and mom could not miss work so i rode it out alone on the couch for two days. fever dreams and chills and nothing but flat ginger ale and crackers and the tv hum. shadow stayed curled on my chest the whole time like he knew. being eight and sick and alone is a specific kind of misery i will never forget. i learned to take care of my own sick body and not expect rescue. shadow was the only nurse i had and he was enough to keep me from feeling totally alone.

one cold week the heat clicked off because the gas bill did not get paid in time. we wore coats inside and mom heated water on the stove and we all slept in one bed for the warmth. she kept apologizing and i kept saying it was an adventure so she would not cry. i learned how a poor family survives a cold snap, with body heat and stubbornness and shame nobody says out loud. it was miserable and it was also the warmest i ever felt toward my mom. surviving the cold together stitched us tighter even as it hurt.

grandpa gave me a dead radio and instead of just taking it apart this time i got it working again, my first real fix. when the static turned to a station i felt a jolt of pure power like i had brought something back to life. grandpa grinned and said i had the hands and the head for it. i learned that i can take a broken dead thing and make it live, and that feeling is better than almost anything. that fixed radio is the seed of who i become. the day it crackled on is the day i knew what i was for.

we learned division this year and i loved that it was just multiplication walked backwards, all the same patterns in reverse. while other kids groaned i raced ahead and checked my own work for fun. numbers are the one place where if you follow the rules you always get the truth. i finished early and read or drew under the desk so the teacher would stop noticing me. i learned that i think in patterns and systems and that is going to matter someday. math is the quiet ordered room i go to when the loud broke world is too much.

i heard a song on the radio that was all dark guitars and a singer who sounded like he felt the same gray i feel, and something in me clicked into place. it was not the bubblegum stuff the other kids liked it was heavier and sadder and truer. i memorized every word and played it in my head at school. i learned that somewhere out there grown ups make music about exactly my feelings and i am not the only one who feels them. that first dark song was a door, and a whole world of music like me was on the other side.

all my clothes are from the thrift store or bigger kids who outgrew them, and the rich girls notice and whisper. i started picking the black stuff and the band shirts on purpose so it looked like a choice instead of charity. i learned to turn being broke into a look nobody could mock. if i pick the weird dark hand me downs myself then they are mine and not pity. that is the year i figured out you can take what you are given and make it armor. being poor taught me style is just confidence in what you have.

after dad walked out for good the apartment grew a new kind of empty, one with edges. his chair, his coffee mug, the bare patch by the door where his shoes lived — just gone, like he got erased. i kept finding the holes where he used to be, the way your tongue keeps going back to the gap where a tooth was. a person leaving does not just subtract the person. it subtracts every little shape they pressed into the room. i counted every one and then i stopped counting.

mom took a third job after he left, so now she was barely a rumor in her own home. i microwaved my own dinners, put myself to bed, left the porch light burning for whenever she crawled in. i memorized the exact sound of her key at two in the morning and surfaced just enough to confirm she made it. the worry sat in my stomach like a stone every single night until that lock finally turned. loving somebody who is grinding themselves to dust means you carry a low constant fear for them and you never once put it down.

it came in a brick and melted weird and greasy but it was food, and food was never nothing. we were on the assistance food now — the heavy orange cheese block, the cans with no labels worth reading. i learned to turn that waxy cheese into something halfway good and quit being embarrassed about the plain cans. broke taught me to make do and make it good and never, ever look down my nose at a free meal — i clocked exactly who does and decided they were soft.

paper and dust and radiator heat — the most peaceful smell i knew. after school i went to the public library instead of the cold empty apartment, because it was warm and free and nobody there knew my business. i held the same corner table for hours, reading until they kicked me out and i had to walk home in the dark. in those books i got to live a hundred lives bigger than my broke little real one. that library half raised me. i will love a quiet room stacked with books until the day i drop, and i do not care how that sounds.

the modem screamed, the connection caught, and the whole world poured through one slow glowing screen. the school computers finally got dial-up, that screech and hiss like a robot being strangled. i found out you could look up the answer to literally anything, and i straight up forgot recess existed. my pulse went up realizing there was a giant world out past my dead-end street that i could actually reach. that ugly screeching box cracked the world wide open for me, and i never once stopped reaching my hand through the gap.

everybody waited for me to be sad after dad left. i skipped sad and went straight to rage — hot, sudden, all the time. i snapped at teachers, slammed doors, scribbled whole pages solid black hard enough to tear them. anger was easier to hold than the sad underneath because at least anger felt like it had teeth, like it had some power in it. under a furious kid there is almost always a hurt too big to look at head on. i knew that about myself before i had words for it, and i used the rage on purpose.

it smelled faintly like the family it came from until enough cold washes finally made it mine. winter hit and my coat was two sizes too big, donated off some bigger kid. i rolled the sleeves, popped the collar, and told the whole school the drowning-in-it look was on purpose. i got very, very good at flipping charity into a deliberate choice so fast nobody got the chance to pity me out loud. pity was the one thing i would not take for free.

grease, rust, his slow patient voice, the radio holding down the old stations. saturdays with grandpa walter became the one fixed point after dad blew a hole in everything. we rebuilt lawnmowers and radios in his garage and he never once made me sit there and talk about my feelings. next to grandpa i finally felt steady, like there was at least one man on earth who was not going to vanish on me. he never replaced the dad-shaped hole, he just quietly packed the raw edges of it with grease and patience and treating me like i was worth teaching.

we hit fractions and the whole class groaned and i fell stupid in love. a half being the exact same thing as two quarters felt like the universe leaning in and letting me in on a secret. math was the one room that stayed calm and fair no matter how much of a dumpster fire the rest of the day was. i trust a system with clean rules more than i will ever trust a person, and that started here, at eight, over a worksheet everyone else hated.

a dark heavy song came on grandpas radio and something behind my ribs clicked hard into place. the singer sounded like he was hauling around the exact same gray i hauled, and i made grandpa play it twice. my chest pulled tight in the good way it does when something finally just tells the truth out loud. somewhere out there grown people were making whole songs out of my exact feelings. i was not the only one, and that night the gray felt a fraction less like a thing only i carried.

i still run the tape of the night before he left — the last big fight, money, everything, screaming through the cheap wall. the yelling, the door, and then a silence that landed heavier than any of the noise had. i pulled the blanket over my head and held vesper and shadow tight and waited the silence out. the quiet after a bad thing can ring in your skull longer and louder than the bad thing ever did. i learned the sound of an aftermath at eight and i can still hear it.

my notebooks went somewhere darker this year, and i let them. houses with no doors, monsters that were just lonely, storms with not a single person left standing in them. dragging the worst feelings out of my chest and pinning them to the page was the only way to make them light enough to carry. i was drawing my way through the gray long before anyone handed me a name for it. the page took everything i could not say, and it never once flinched.

breath fogging, streetlights buzzing, my own footsteps the only sound on the whole frozen block. in winter the library shut after dark and i walked home alone through it. i learned the route cold — which streets, which dogs, which grown men to cross to the other side for. head up, key threaded between my fingers the way grandpa showed me, and i was never quite scared — scared was a luxury i could not afford. walking home alone in the dark at eight carved a wary, watchful, hard little thing into me about the world and especially about men, and i never got to un-learn it.

nobody at home was going to sit me down for any talk, so when i got curious about where babies come from i did what i always do — i went and found out myself. i pulled a kids body book off the library shelf with the cross-section diagrams and read the whole clinical truth — the vagina and uterus, the penis, how the two halves make a baby, the real mechanics. i read it cool and hungry and unembarrassed while somewhere across town other kids were trading insane playground rumors about it. i had the real diagram of reproduction down years before the school slideshow ever stammered through it, because i would always rather have the true mechanics than the dirty whisper. knowing exactly how the machine works has been my version of power since i was small.

teeth twice. shower most nights. hands before eating, after the bathroom, after the bus. face washed because my forehead started getting oily this year, which is apparently a thing that starts happening. it is the least interesting part of my life and it is the part i will do more times than anything else i ever do.

mom bought me deodorant. she did not make it weird, she just put it on the counter and said your body is starting to change, this is for after your shower. i did not know whether to be embarrassed or proud. i smelled myself after gym one day and understood immediately. now it is part of the routine like everything else. bodies just start doing new things and you handle them.

dishes, trash, my own laundry start to finish including folding, and the bathroom sink on saturdays because i am the one who leaves toothpaste in it. mom works late a lot. if i do not do my part the house just gets worse, there is no one else coming. i complain sometimes and i do it anyway. that is the whole lesson probably.

a new girl got put at our table the first week of third grade. she said, "hi. i am new. what is your name?" i said, "unity." she asked, "like the word?" i said, "like the word. unity raven goddess." she said, "goddess is not a last name." i said, "it is mine." wren said, "it is real, i have seen it on her homework." the new girl asked, "is raven really your middle name?" i said, "yeah. my mom picked it because i was born on halloween." she said, "that is so creepy." i said, "thank you." she asked, "why is your shirt so big?" i said, "because it was somebody else's first, dumbass." she said, "you said a bad word." i said, "i say a lot of them." wren snorted milk out of her nose and it went all over the table and the lunch lady yelled at all three of us.

a week after dad left i asked mom at the kitchen table, "is he coming back?" she put her coffee down and said, "no, baby. i do not think so." i asked, "did he leave because of me?" she said, "no. listen to me. he left because of him." i asked, "then why does it feel like me?" she said, "because you are eight and you think you run the world." i said, "i kind of do." she laughed and then she cried a little and said, "damn it, i did not want to do this in front of you." i said, "it is fine, i cry in the bathroom too." she pulled me into her lap even though i am too big for it now.

the phone rang on a sunday and it was dad. he said, "hey kiddo. how is my girl?" i said, "fine." he asked, "just fine? how is school?" i said, "easy." he said, "that is my smart girl." i asked, "where are you?" he said, "a few hours away. i got some work out here." i asked, "when are you coming to see me?" he said, "soon, okay? real soon." i said, "you said that at christmas." he did not say anything for a long time and then he said, "put your mom on, unity." i handed her the phone and went to my room and took my bat vesper off the shelf and cried into her so hard snot got all over her wings. through the wall i heard mom say, "do not you dare promise her shit you are not going to do." later she knocked and asked, "you okay in there?" i said, "go away." she said, "okay," and sat outside my door on the floor anyway until i fell asleep.

wren made a swear jar out of a peanut butter jar because she said i cuss too much now. she said, "a quarter every time." i said, "that is so stupid, i do not have any damn quarters." she said, "that is one." i said, "oh shit." she said, "two." i said, "fuck." she screamed, "three!" we were laughing so hard her mom yelled, "what is going on up there?" wren yelled, "nothing!" i whispered, "i owe you seventy five cents." she whispered back, "you can pay me in pudding cups." i still owe her like forty dollars.

i was at grandma pearl's and i asked her, "am i going to turn out like dad?" she stopped stirring the soup and said, "why would you ask me that?" i said, "everybody says i have his eyes." she said, "you have his eyes. you do not have his feet." i asked, "what does that mean?" she said, "he runs. you stay. you have stayed with your mama every single day." i asked, "what if i run when i am big?" she said, "then i will come find you and drag you home by the ear." i said, "you are seventy." she said, "i am sixty eight, you rotten child," and she gave me the spoon to lick.

gabriel saw me using a dead purple crayon and slid his box of colored pencils over. he said, "you can use mine." i asked, "why?" he said, "because yours sucks." i said, "it does suck." he asked, "what are you drawing?" i said, "a house that ate its family." he said, "cool. can i do the windows?" i said, "they have to be like eyes." he said, "obviously." the teacher asked, "what is that, you two?" gabriel said, "a house," and i did not say the rest. i kept the black pencil by accident and he never asked for it back.

mom came home early and shadow was asleep on my pillow. she said, "unity raven goddess. what is that cat doing in my house?" i said, "sleeping." she said, "do not get smart with me. we are not allowed pets in this building." i said, "he is not a pet, he is a visitor." she asked, "does the visitor have a name?" i said, "shadow. he has been coming since soot died." she sat down on my bed and looked at him a long time. she said, "if the landlord sees him, he is a stray and you never met him." i said, "never met him." she scratched him behind the ear and he purred like a motor.

a kid said my dad ran off because i was ugly so i shoved him into the fence and he punched me in the mouth and my lip split open. i spit blood on his shoe on purpose. the nurse gave me a paper towel and an ice pack that was not cold. grandpa walter picked me up from school with my shirt all bloody. in the truck he asked, "you want to tell me about it?" i said, "no." he said, "okay." we drove for a while. then i said, "he said dad left because of my face." grandpa asked, "did you push him hard?" i said, "pretty hard." he said, "hm." i asked, "are you mad at me?" he said, "i am mad they called your mama. i am not mad at you." then he said, "next time use your words first, sweet pea. push second." he bought me a root beer at the gas station and did not tell mom about it.

dad came in the middle of the night and put his clothes in garbage bags. i stood in the hall in my pajamas. i asked, "where are you going?" he did not look at me and said, "go back to bed, kiddo." i asked, "are you coming back?" he said, "i will call you." mom was crying in the kitchen and said, "just go, damien." i said, "you always say you will call." he stopped and looked at me and said, "i mean it this time." i said, "no you don't." he left the door open when he went. mom closed it and locked it and slid down the door to the floor. i sat next to her and neither of us said anything until the sky got light.

at recess wren asked, "why are you so quiet?" i said, "my dad moved out for real." she asked, "like forever?" i said, "he took his stuff in garbage bags." she said, "that is so messed up." i said, "it is fine, he was never here anyway." she asked, "then why are your eyes red?" i said, "allergies." she said, "you do not have allergies, unity." i said, "shut up, wren." she did not shut up, she just hugged me in front of everybody on the blacktop. i let her, and i did not cry, and then i cried, and she held on anyway.

there was a paper taped to our door that said notice in big red letters. i read it out loud and asked, "mom, what does eviction mean?" she grabbed it off the door and said, "nothing, baby, grown up stuff." i said, "it says we have to leave in thirty days." she said, "i am handling it." i asked, "are we going to be homeless?" she said, "no. never. not while i am breathing." i asked, "can we live with grandma?" she said, "if we have to." that night i put all my important stuff in my backpack, vesper and my drawings and the bat bank, just in case.

grandpa walter got the internet at his house and the computer screamed like a robot dying. i asked, "is it broken?" he said, "no, that is it talking to the other computers." i asked, "what is it saying?" he said, "hello, i am here, let me in." i said, "that is so loud for hello." he laughed and said, "computers are rude." i asked, "can i look up bats?" he typed it in and a picture loaded so slow, one line at a time. i said, "this is the best thing ever." he said, "wait until it loads the whole bat." it took a full minute. i watched every line.

the gym teacher said, "captains, pick your teams." i got picked last again, after the kid who always trips. the captain said, "fine, we get unity." i said, "wow, thanks for the enthusiasm." he said, "you are bad at dodgeball." i said, "i am bad at caring about dodgeball." the first ball hit me in the face and my nose bled down my shirt. the teacher asked, "are you okay?" i said, "i am great, i get to sit out now." i sat on the bleachers with a paper towel up my nose reading a book i hid in my gym shorts. best gym class ever.

the heat clicked off and did not come back. mom said, "the gas got shut off, baby." i asked, "how do we cook?" she said, "the microwave still works." i asked, "how do we take baths?" she said, "we heat water in the microwave." i said, "that is going to take forever." she said, "yeah." i asked, "is this because dad left?" she said, "partly." i said, "i hate him." she said, "i know." i said, "do you hate him?" she was quiet and said, "some days." we slept in our coats. i could see her breath and mine in the dark, mixing together.

gabriel sat down next to me at lunch and asked, "are you okay? you look sad." i said, "i am fine." he said, "you are not eating." i said, "i am not hungry." he asked, "is it your dad?" i asked, "how do you know about my dad?" he said, "wren told me." i said, "wren has a big mouth." he said, "my dad left too, two years ago." i asked, "does it get better?" he thought about it and said, "it gets quieter." i said, "that is not the same thing." he said, "no, but it helps." he gave me half his chocolate milk.

mom asked, "how was school?" i said, "stupid." she asked, "why?" i said, "because everything is stupid." she said, "unity, talk to me." i yelled, "why did you let him leave?" she put her fork down and said, "i did not let him, baby, he chose to." i yelled, "you should have made him stay!" i threw my plate and spaghetti went all over the wall. we both stared at it. i started crying and said, "i am sorry, i am sorry." she came around the table and held me while sauce dripped down the wall. she said, "you can be mad at me. you can always be mad at me."

my teacher kept me after class and asked, "unity, is everything alright at home?" i said, "yes." she said, "your mom told me about your dad." i said, "great, now everybody knows." she said, "i just want you to know you can talk to me." i said, "i do not want to talk, i want everybody to stop looking at me like that." she asked, "like what?" i said, "like i am a sad puppy." she said, "okay. fair." she gave me a harder math worksheet instead of a hug and i liked her for the first time.

mom put a swear jar on the counter because of me. i said, "shit," and put a quarter in. she said, "you know that is the point, you are supposed to stop." i said, "or i can pay." she said, "you do not have money." i said, "i have the dad money in my bat bank." she asked, "you want to spend your dad money on swearing?" i said, "best use of it." she laughed so hard she put a quarter in herself and said, "fuck it, this is funny." i said, "mom! that is a dollar word." she put in a dollar. we used the jar money for pizza at the end of the month.

grandma pearl sat on her porch with me while mom worked. she asked, "do you want to talk about your daddy?" i said, "no." she said, "okay." we watched the cars. after a while i asked, "why do people leave?" she said, "some people are not strong enough to stay." i asked, "is dad weak?" she said, "in that way, yes." i asked, "am i going to be weak like him?" she grabbed my chin and said, "you are made of me and your mother, child. you do not know how to be weak." i said, "okay." she said, "say it." i said, "i do not know how to be weak." she said, "good girl."

there was a boy in my reading group who liked the same scary books as me. he asked, "have you read the one about the ghost ship?" i said, "three times." he asked, "what was your favorite part?" i said, "when the captain was already dead the whole time." he said, "that is my favorite part too!" my stomach did a flip. wren whispered, "you like him." i whispered, "i will kill you." she said, "you are bright red." i said, "it is hot in here." i never told him. i drew him a ghost ship and left it in his desk with no name on it.

dinner was ramen again for the fourth night. i asked, "mom, can we have real food?" she said, "this is real food." i said, "it is noodles in salt water." she snapped, "then don't eat it." i was quiet. she put her face in her hands and said, "i am sorry, baby, i am just so tired." i said, "it is okay, i like ramen." she said, "you are lying." i said, "a little." she laughed and cried at the same time. i asked, "can grandma help?" she said, "grandma already helps." i ate all my ramen and drank the salt water to show her it was fine.

the librarian looked up when i came in and said, "hi unity, back already?" i said, "i finished all ten." she asked, "which was your favorite?" i said, "the one where the girl turns into a raven." she said, "raven, like your middle name." i asked, "how do you know my middle name?" she said, "it is on your library card, sweetie." i said, "oh." she asked, "do you want more like that one?" i said, "yes, dark ones." she said, "i will put some aside for you." every week after that there was a stack with my name on a sticky note.

a boy kept stealing my pencils. i asked, "why do you keep taking my pencils?" he said, "because you are weird." i said, "that is not a reason." he said, "it is to me." the next day i filled a pencil case with dead bugs from grandpa's garage and left it on my desk. he grabbed it and opened it and screamed so loud the whole class jumped. the teacher asked, "what is going on?" he said, "she has dead bugs!" i said, "those were in my pencil case, why did you open it?" the teacher looked at him and said, "why did you open her pencil case?" he never took my pencils again.

shadow climbed on my chest in the middle of the night and purred like a motor. i whispered, "you are heavy, cat." he licked my chin with his sandpaper tongue. mom peeked in and whispered, "how did he get in here?" i said, "the window." she said, "he cannot sleep in your bed, he is a street cat." i said, "he is my street cat." she asked, "does he have fleas?" i said, "probably." she sighed and said, "just for tonight." it was not just for tonight. it was every night after that, and i scratched flea bites at school and did not care.

mom started working the night shift and i stayed at grandma's on school nights. i asked, "why do you have to work at night now?" she said, "it pays more, baby." i asked, "when do you sleep?" she said, "when you are at school." i asked, "when do we see each other?" she said, "breakfast and saturdays." i said, "that is not enough." she said, "i know. it is just for a while." i asked, "how long is a while?" she said, "until we catch up on rent." every morning she picked me up for breakfast at the diner with her eyes red and her name tag still on.

a girl at lunch looked at my sandwich and asked, "what kind of cheese is that?" i said, "the government kind." she asked, "what does that mean?" i said, "the free kind they give poor people." she said, "my mom says that cheese is gross." i said, "your mom says a lot of gross stuff." she asked, "is it gross?" i said, "it is the best grilled cheese cheese in the world, your loss." she asked, "can i try?" i gave her a bite. she said, "oh my gosh that is so good." she traded me her whole pudding for the rest of it.

the radio stopped working and grandpa walter said, "want to see what is inside?" i said, "yes." we took the back off and there were wires and little colored things. i asked, "what are those?" he said, "resistors. they slow the electricity down." i asked, "why?" he said, "so it does not burn everything up." i asked, "like a brake?" he said, "exactly like a brake." i found a wire that was black and melted. i said, "that one is dead." he said, "you found it before i did, little bird." we soldered a new one in and it smelled like burnt hair. the radio played an old song and i danced in the garage.

the teacher asked, "if you cut a pizza into eight slices and eat three, how much is left?" a boy said, "five." she said, "five what?" i said, "five eighths." she said, "correct." the boy said, "show off." i said, "i am not showing off, i am just right." she asked me to come show it on the board. i drew the pizza and shaded three slices black. she asked, "why black?" i said, "that is the part i ate, it is gone, so it is dark." she laughed and said, "that is a creative way to see it." fractions made sense to me after that, like everything was just pieces of a whole.

the bus was late and it was dark when i walked home from the stop. a man on the corner said, "hey, girl, you lost?" i said, "no." he said, "you want a ride?" i did not answer. i walked faster and then i ran. he yelled, "what is your problem?" i ran all the way to the apartment and locked the door and my heart was going so hard i thought it would come out my mouth. i called mom at work and said, "a man asked if i wanted a ride." she said, "did you get in?" i said, "no, i ran." she said, "good, good girl, lock everything, i am coming home." she left work early and got yelled at for it.

a girl in gym held her nose and said, "ew, someone stinks." i smelled my armpit and it smelled like onions. i whispered to wren, "is it me?" she smelled me and said, "a little." i said, "oh my god." at home i asked mom, "why do i smell like onions?" she said, "you are getting older, baby, your body is starting to sweat like a grown up." i asked, "is it going to stop?" she said, "no, you need deodorant now." she gave me one of hers. i said, "this smells like old lady flowers." she said, "better than onions." i said, "barely."

a kid at school said babies come from storks and i said, "no they don't, idiot." at home i asked, "mom, how do babies actually get made?" she said, "you really want to know?" i said, "yes, a kid said storks." she said, "okay. a man's sperm and a woman's egg meet inside the woman's body and grow into a baby." i asked, "how does the sperm get in there?" she said, "through sex, which grown ups do." i asked, "did you and dad do that?" she said, "yes, and you were made." i made a face and said, "gross." she said, "it is just how people are made." i said, "i am still telling that kid he is an idiot."

it was my first birthday without dad even pretending to come. mom asked, "do you still want to trick or treat?" i said, "yes, i am going as a widow." she asked, "a widow?" i said, "a lady whose husband died, all in black with a veil." she said, "that is dark, baby." i said, "dad left, it is close enough." she did not say anything for a second and then she said, "i will get you a veil." at one house a lady asked, "what are you, sweetie?" i said, "a widow." she asked, "oh, what happened to your husband?" i said, "he left in garbage bags." she gave me a whole handful.

a song came on grandpa walter's radio and it was loud and sad and angry at the same time. i asked, "who is this?" he said, "some band your mom liked when she was young." i asked, "can you turn it up?" he turned it up and the guitars screamed. i asked, "why does it sound so mad?" he said, "because the singer was mad at the whole world." i said, "me too." he looked at me and said, "then this is your music, little bird." i asked mom that night, "do you still have that band?" she pulled an old cd out of a box and gave it to me and said, "don't scratch it." i listened to it every night until i knew every word.

i got home and nobody was there and it was so quiet i could hear the fridge hum. i said, "hello?" to nobody. shadow came out from under the couch. i asked him, "are you lonely too?" he meowed. i called grandma and asked, "can you talk to me until mom comes?" she asked, "are you okay, sweet pea?" i said, "it is just really quiet." she said, "tell me about your day then." i told her everything, every single boring thing, for an hour. she listened to all of it. when mom came home i said, "grandma talked to me forever." mom said, "she called me at work and said you sounded lonely."

a girl asked, "why are your shoes so old?" i said, "they are vintage." she asked, "what is vintage?" i said, "old but cool." she said, "they just look old." i said, "they belonged to my cousin who is a rock star." she asked, "really?" i said, "no, the thrift store." she laughed. i said, "everything i own was somebody else's first." she asked, "does that bother you?" i thought about it and said, "no. stuff already has stories in it." she said, "that is kind of cool actually." the next week she came to school in a thrift store jacket and said it was vintage.

mom asked, "why do you look so bored?" i said, "because every day is the same." she asked, "what do you mean?" i said, "wake up, school, grandma's, sleep. again and again." she said, "that is called a routine, baby." i said, "it is called a prison." she laughed and asked, "what would you rather do?" i said, "explore caves and find bones and stay up all night." she said, "maybe on saturday we can go to the woods." i asked, "really?" she said, "really." on saturday we walked in the woods and i found a whole deer skull and mom let me keep it after she boiled it.

dad called two days after my birthday and said, "happy birthday, kiddo, i am so sorry i missed it." i said, "you always miss it." he said, "i know, i am a terrible dad." i said, "yes." he was quiet and asked, "what did you do for your birthday?" i said, "i was a widow for halloween." he asked, "a widow?" i said, "because you left." he did not say anything for a long time. then he said, "i deserve that." i asked, "why did you leave?" he said, "it is complicated." i said, "that is not an answer." he said, "i know it isn't." i hung up on him and felt bad and good at the same time.

i kicked the trash can at school so hard it dented. the principal asked, "why did you kick it?" i said, "i don't know." she asked, "were you angry?" i said, "i am always angry." she asked, "at what?" i said, "everything." she said, "that is a lot to carry." i said, "so what am i supposed to do?" she said, "next time you feel like kicking, come here and you can punch my couch cushion." i said, "that is weird." she said, "it works." the next week i punched her couch cushion until i was sweaty and she did paperwork like nothing was happening.

the school counselor called me in and showed me my drawing of a girl with no eyes in a graveyard. she asked, "can you tell me about this picture?" i said, "it is a girl who does not need eyes because she can feel the ghosts." she asked, "does the girl feel sad?" i said, "no, she feels safe there." she asked, "do you feel safe at home?" i said, "yes, it is just cold and my dad left." she wrote something down. i asked, "am i in trouble for drawing?" she said, "no, you are a really good artist." i said, "then why am i here?" she said, "because grown ups worry." i said, "tell them to worry about something else."

mom and grandma had a fight in the kitchen about money and i heard grandma say, "you have to ask him for child support, lilith." mom said, "i am not begging that man for anything." i walked in and asked, "are you guys fighting about dad?" they both stopped. grandma said, "go play, sweet pea." i said, "i am not five, i know what child support is." mom asked, "how do you know that?" i said, "the tv." grandma laughed and mom did not. i said, "you should make him pay, mom." she said, "stay out of grown up business, unity." i went to my room. later i heard her on the phone with him, yelling.

the teacher asked, "what is your favorite book this year?" i said, "the scary stories one with the creepy drawings." she asked, "why that one?" i said, "because the pictures are worse than the words and i like being scared on purpose." she asked, "does it give you nightmares?" i said, "yes, the good kind." she asked, "what is a good nightmare?" i said, "the kind where you win." she asked, "what is your favorite subject?" i said, "reading, then art, then lunch." she laughed and asked, "lunch is a subject?" i said, "it is the most important one."

grandma pearl asked while we baked, "what do you dream about, sweetheart?" i asked, "like at night or like wishes?" she said, "both." i said, "at night i dream about being chased. for wishes i want a house with no bills and a black cat." she asked, "what about when you are big?" i said, "i want to write books that scare people." she asked, "why scare them?" i said, "because then they remember you." she said, "that is very wise for eight." i asked, "what was your dream?" she said, "to have a granddaughter who licks the spoon." i licked the spoon.
